title: Warsh shows why quality trumps quantity in central bank communications
gist: Capital Economics' Neil Shearing argues Kevin Warsh's debut FOMC press appearance undercut his own case for scaling back Fed communications: the 'play the ball, not the referee' analogy misreads a central bank that sets the rules rather than interpreting them, and markets responded by pricing a less hawkish near term while selling long-dated Treasuries on longer-run inflation risk. Drawing on Mervyn King's Maradona theory and the Bank of England's Goodhart's-Law failure with unemployment-threshold guidance, he concludes that cutting FOMC meetings from eight to six matters far less than the quality of communication at each remaining one.

insights.claim: New Fed chair Kevin Warsh attributed the rise in nominal and real long-dated Treasury yields since June to investors 'learning to play the ball, not the referee' - i.e. responding to economic data rather than anticipating the Fed.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: The Fed chair is publicly reframing the long-end selloff as data-driven rather than policy-driven, which lowers the odds he responds to it - a reason to keep term-premium risk on the table.
insights.quote: “learning to play the ball, not the referee”
insights.locator: The Chairman's muddles

insights.claim: The 'referee' analogy for the Fed is fundamentally misplaced because the central bank does not interpret the rules - it sets one of them by determining short-term interest rates, so incoming data only matter insofar as they shape the Fed's response.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Treat any 'the data, not the Fed, is driving markets' narrative as rhetorical cover; the reaction function still dominates pricing across the curve.
insights.quote: The central bank is, by design, the centre of attention.
insights.locator: The analogy is fundamentally misplaced.

insights.claim: Warsh's stated view that central banks need not always be the centre of attention misunderstands the Fed's role, since markets exist precisely to price how the Fed will set short-term rates.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: A Fed chair who wants less market attention on the Fed will likely under-supply guidance, raising realised rate volatility around each meeting.
insights.quote: “central banks need not always and everywhere be the centre of attention”
insights.locator: Warsh went on to say that

themes.theme: Unusual bond-market reaction to the FOMC

insights.claim: After the Fed's mixed messaging, investors simultaneously pared back expectations for near-term rate hikes and sold longer-dated bonds - pricing a less hawkish Fed in the short run but greater inflation risk over the longer term.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: That combination is a curve-steepener signature; watch 2s30s for follow-through as a market verdict on Fed credibility rather than on the data.
insights.quote: pricing a less hawkish Fed in the short run but greater inflation risks over the longer term
insights.locator: Markets understandably struggled to reconcile

insights.claim: The simultaneous dovish-front-end / hawkish-long-end move was a relatively unusual response to an FOMC meeting, benchmarked against changes in 2-year and 30-year Treasury yields on FOMC announcement days since 1994.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Outlier FOMC-day reactions flag a communications failure rather than a data surprise - a marker that the new chair's guidance is not yet anchoring expectations.
insights.quote: Chart 1: Changes In 2-yr and 30-yr Treasury Yields On FOMC Announcement Days Since 1994 (bp)
insights.locator: That relatively unusual response to an FOMC meeting

insights.claim: The bond market's response was a poor outcome for a Fed chair who had spent the previous month trying to assert his inflation-fighting credentials.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Failed credential-building raises the chance of an over-correction toward hawkishness at the next meeting to reclaim the inflation narrative.
insights.locator: That relatively unusual response to an FOMC meeting

insights.claim: Forward guidance sits on a spectrum: at the light end policymakers merely signal how they expect policy to evolve over coming months in order to move financial conditions; at the strong end they explicitly commit not to adjust policy until specified economic conditions are met.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Classify any new Fed guidance by where it sits on this spectrum - only the conditional-commitment end meaningfully compresses front-end rate volatility.
insights.locator: Forward guidance exists on a spectrum.

insights.claim: Neither the light-touch signalling form of forward guidance nor the strong conditional-commitment form is as effective in practice as either its supporters or its critics claim.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Do not price a large regime shift in rate volatility from a Fed that guides less - the marginal effect of guidance in either direction has been overstated.
insights.quote: neither form of forward guidance is quite as effective as either its supporters or its critics suggest
insights.locator: In practice, however

insights.claim: The Bank of England's 2013 experiment in strong forward guidance pledged not to raise interest rates above the ultra-accommodative level of 0.5% until the unemployment rate fell to 7%.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: This is the concrete precedent - and failure mode - against which any future Fed threshold-based guidance should be judged.
insights.locator: The latter approach was adopted by the Bank of England in 2013

themes.theme: Maradona theory and the credibility limit

insights.claim: Mervyn King's 'Maradona theory' of central banking holds that a central bank can achieve the desired tightening or loosening of financial conditions purely by shaping expectations, without actually changing interest rates - just as Maradona ran nearly straight at goal while feinting defenders out of his way in 1986.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: A useful lens for reading Fed speak: verbal tightening substitutes for hikes, so financial conditions can move well ahead of any actual policy change.
insights.quote: central banks can sometimes achieve the desired tightening or loosening in financial conditions simply by shaping expectations, without actually changing interest rates
insights.locator: Maradona revisited

insights.claim: Expectations management has a hard credibility limit: if policymakers repeatedly hint that rates will rise but fail to deliver, inflation expectations may drift higher and currencies may weaken, forcing them to act anyway - and the same logic runs in reverse for signalled easing.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Watch breakevens and FX as the tripwires that convert cheap talk into forced policy action; persistent gaps between rhetoric and delivery are tradeable.
insights.quote: Markets eventually test central banks’ resolve.
insights.locator: But there are limits to this strategy.

insights.claim: The Bank of England's unemployment-threshold guidance was ultimately undermined by structural changes in the labour market that let unemployment fall without generating the wage pressure and inflation policymakers had expected.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Any single-indicator policy threshold is hostage to structural shifts in that indicator - a reason to fade guidance tied to one labour-market statistic.
insights.locator: Its decision to make interest rate hikes conditional

insights.claim: Once the unemployment rate became the Bank of England's policy threshold, markets shifted weight away from unemployment data toward wage and inflation data and kept pricing ultra-loose policy even as unemployment fell - a textbook case of Goodhart's Law.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: When a central bank names a target variable, reposition around the variables it did not name - that is where the information migrates.
insights.quote: once a particular measure becomes the target of policy, it stops being a reliable measure
insights.locator: Goodhart’s trap

themes.theme: Cutting FOMC meetings from eight to six

insights.claim: Media reports indicate the new Fed chair is considering cutting the number of scheduled FOMC meetings per year from the current eight to perhaps six.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Fewer scheduled decision dates concentrate event risk - reprice options and hedges around a shorter calendar of higher-variance Fed days.
insights.locator: Fewer meetings, same challenge

insights.claim: There is nothing sacrosanct about eight FOMC meetings a year: by law the FOMC need only meet four times, the count varied historically before settling at eight under Paul Volcker, and six would still exceed the quarterly Swiss National Bank while trailing the ECB and Bank of England at eight.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: The proposed cut sits well within international norms, so treat headlines about it as noise rather than an institutional rupture.
insights.locator: There is nothing sacrosanct about the current eight annual meetings.

insights.claim: Kevin Warsh's own 2014 review of the Bank of England's operations led the BoE to cut its policy meetings from 12 to eight, meaning his Fed meeting-reduction agenda follows a precedent he personally authored.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: This is a long-held Warsh conviction rather than an improvisation, raising the probability the Fed change actually happens.
insights.quote: the Bank of England cut the number of its policy meetings from 12 following a recommendation in Kevin Warsh's 2014 review of its operations
insights.locator: Indeed, the Bank of England cut the number

insights.claim: The trade-off from fewer policy meetings is that policymakers are less tempted to tinker but slower to respond to shocks, and the emergency-meeting fallback hits markets harder by creating the impression that policymakers know something investors do not.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: In a six-meeting regime an unscheduled FOMC becomes a much larger tail event; price inter-meeting risk accordingly.
insights.quote: they can have a much greater impact on markets, creating the impression that policymakers know something investors do not
insights.locator: The trade-off, however

insights.claim: Fewer meetings would not by themselves materially change the conduct of monetary policy, but because each remaining meeting carries greater weight they raise the premium on clear and consistent communication - a standard the Fed under its new chairman is not currently meeting.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: The investable risk is communication quality, not meeting count: expect wider dispersion in rate expectations and fatter FOMC-day moves.
insights.quote: If the Fed communicates less frequently, each meeting carries greater weight.
insights.locator: The bigger concern is the backdrop

insights.claim: Recent US data point to stronger underlying demand and persistent inflation pressures, making a September Fed rate hike more likely than not despite the confusion around Fed communications.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: A live September hike against a market that just pared near-term hike expectations is the clearest asymmetric front-end trade in the piece.
insights.quote: a September rate hike remains more likely than not
insights.locator: In case you missed it

insights.claim: Emerging-market economies are generally weathering the Middle East conflict according to the latest EM Financial Risk Indicators, but higher energy prices are leaving some exposed.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Screen EM by energy-import exposure rather than treating the bloc as uniformly resilient to the conflict.
insights.locator: The latest update of our EM Financial Risk Indicators

insights.claim: News of advances in Chinese chipmaking is being treated as a materially consequential follow-on to China's broader progress in AI.
insights.speaker: Neil Shearing
insights.so_what: Chinese chip self-sufficiency progress is a direct risk to the export-control moat underpinning Western AI-hardware valuations.
insights.locator: Following last week’s Drop-In on China’s progress in AI
